title: env
text:
This module answers two questions every release step runs into: where a project’s tokens and settings are kept, and what environment a child command should run with.
An environment value is any named setting a build or a deploy needs, such as GITHUB_TOKEN or PORT. Some of them are secrets that should not sit in plain text. EnvStore keeps them through dockeasy, which puts secrets in the system keychain and every value in an env file (~/.config/fastops/.env unless you name another). dockeasy is imported the first time a value is read or written, not when this module loads.


source

EnvError
def EnvError(
    *args, **kwargs
):
Unspecified run-time error.


When pullup runs inside a frozen desktop app, one built with py2app or a similar tool, the app’s launcher sets variables such as PYTHONHOME that point Python at the copy bundled inside the app. A child process that inherits them starts the wrong interpreter. BUNDLE_ONLY lists those variables. EnvError is raised when a value cannot be stored, or when dockeasy, which does the storing, is not installed.


source

clean_env
def clean_env():
A copy of this process’s environment with the frozen-app interpreter variables removed.




source

strip_bundle
def strip_bundle(
    env, frozen:NoneType=None
):
Remove the frozen-app interpreter variables from env when running frozen, and return it.


strip_bundle removes the BUNDLE_ONLY variables from an environment mapping and sets PYTHONUTF8=1. It changes the mapping you pass and returns that same mapping. By default it only does this when the current process is frozen; pass frozen=True or frozen=False to decide yourself, as the example does. clean_env covers the common case: a copy of this process’s environment with the bundle variables always removed.

env = {'PYTHONHOME': '/Pullup.app/Contents/Resources', 'PATH': '/usr/bin', 'HOME': '/Users/me'}
strip_bundle(dict(env), frozen=True)

{'PATH': '/usr/bin', 'HOME': '/Users/me', 'PYTHONUTF8': '1'}




source

venv_env
def venv_env(
    python:NoneType=None, env:NoneType=None
):
A copy of env that runs commands in the virtual environment of python, or unchanged when python is None.


venv_env returns an environment that runs commands inside a particular virtual environment, much as source .venv/bin/activate would. Pass the path of that environment’s Python. It copies the mapping, sets VIRTUAL_ENV, puts the interpreter’s directory first on PATH, and drops PYTHONHOME and UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT, either of which would send commands to a different interpreter. With no python the mapping comes back as a copy, passed only through strip_bundle.

e = venv_env('/repo/.venv/bin/python', env={'PATH': '/usr/bin', 'PYTHONHOME': '/frozen'})
e['VIRTUAL_ENV'], e['PATH'], 'PYTHONHOME' in e

('/repo/.venv', '/repo/.venv/bin:/usr/bin', False)




source

needs_extra
def needs_extra(
    what
):
An error message for what that ends with the command that installs the missing library.




source

extra
def extra():
The package name that missing-library errors tell the reader to install.




source

use_extra
def use_extra(
    name
):
Set the package name that missing-library errors tell the reader to install.


Some of pullup’s features need another library, and the error raised when it is missing ends with the command that installs it. use_extra changes the package named in that command. A host application that bundles pullup calls it so that the message names the host’s own package. needs_extra builds the message and extra returns the name in use.
_dockeasy imports the four dockeasy functions the store uses, or raises EnvError with the install hint. Some dockeasy versions return coroutines from these functions, so _call runs whatever comes back to completion. It works whether or not an event loop is already running, which is the case inside Jupyter, and it re-raises any exception the call raised.

async def double(x): return x*2
_call(double, 21), _call(lambda x: x*2, 21)

(42, 42)




source

EnvStore
def EnvStore(
    service:str='fastops', path:NoneType=None
):
Read and write one project’s tokens and settings through dockeasy’s keychain and env file.


EnvStore reads and writes the values for one project.

get asks dockeasy for the key. For a secret dockeasy checks the keychain, then this process’s environment, then the env file; for an ordinary value it skips the keychain. A key found nowhere returns ''.
set with secret=True, the default, writes the value to the keychain under service and to the env file. With secret=False it writes to the env file only. Either way dockeasy also puts it in os.environ.
unset removes a key from the keychain, the env file and os.environ, and reports which of the first two held it.
values reads several keys at once and leaves out the ones with no value. This is what a pipeline hands to a child process.


store = EnvStore(path=envfile)
store.set('PULLUP_DEMO_REGISTRY', 'ghcr.io/example', secret=False)
store.get('PULLUP_DEMO_REGISTRY', secret=False)

'ghcr.io/example'


The examples use secret=False, so nothing touches the keychain.

store.values(['PULLUP_DEMO_REGISTRY', 'PULLUP_DEMO_TAG'], secret=False)

{'PULLUP_DEMO_REGISTRY': 'ghcr.io/example'}



store.unset('PULLUP_DEMO_REGISTRY')

{'key': 'PULLUP_DEMO_REGISTRY', 'removed': ['env file']}




source

env_value
def env_value(
    store, key, default:str='', secret:bool=False
):
One value from an environment store, or default when it is unset or the store raises.


env_value is the forgiving read. It returns default when the key is unset and also when the store raises, for example because the keychain is locked. Unlike EnvStore.get, it reads ordinary values unless you pass secret=True. Use it wherever a missing value has a sensible fallback.

env_value(store, 'PULLUP_DEMO_REGISTRY', 'ghcr.io/fallback')

'ghcr.io/fallback'

title: infra
text:
A deployed app lives on a Hetzner server behind a Cloudflare tunnel. This module lists and cleans up those resources: servers through vpseasy, and tunnels, zones and DNS records through cfeasy. It reads the API tokens, HCLOUD_TOKEN and CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, from the project’s environment store, so you do not have to export them first.


source

InfraError
def InfraError(
    *args, **kwargs
):
Unspecified run-time error.


InfraError is the error meant to be shown to a person: a library that is missing, a token that is not set, a name that does not exist. A failure from the provider or the network keeps its own type, and overview reports the two differently.
vpseasy’s Hetzner client reads HCLOUD_TOKEN from the process environment when it is created. _with_env sets values in os.environ for the length of a with block and then puts back what was there before, removing keys that did not exist. Empty values are not set:

os.environ['PULLUP_DEMO'] = 'before'
with _with_env({'PULLUP_DEMO': 'during', 'PULLUP_ABSENT': 'x'}):
    inside = os.environ['PULLUP_DEMO'], os.environ['PULLUP_ABSENT']
inside, os.environ['PULLUP_DEMO'], 'PULLUP_ABSENT' in os.environ

(('during', 'x'), 'before', False)


The values are restored even when the block raises, which matters because creating a client is what runs inside it.
_record turns a Cloudflare DNS record into a flat row. Missing text fields become empty strings and ttl is kept as given. tunnel is true when the record’s content ends in .cfargotunnel.com, the address of a Cloudflare tunnel:

_record({'id': 'a1', 'type': 'CNAME', 'name': 'app.example.com',
         'content': '9f2b.cfargotunnel.com', 'proxied': True, 'ttl': 1})

{'id': 'a1',
 'type': 'CNAME',
 'name': 'app.example.com',
 'content': '9f2b.cfargotunnel.com',
 'proxied': True,
 'ttl': 1,
 'tunnel': True}


installed says whether a module can be found, which is not the same as whether it imports: a package whose code fails at import time is found, and then breaks at the call. _why tells the two apart, so the install hint is only offered when installing would help.


source

Infra
def Infra(
    env:NoneType=None
):
Hetzner servers and Cloudflare tunnels, zones and DNS records, using this project’s tokens.


When vpseasy or cfeasy is installed but fails to import, Infra raises InfraError with the import failure attached as its cause.
Infra looks each token up itself: in the environment store first, then in this process’s environment, and '' when neither has it. A store that raises, such as a locked keychain, is passed over and the environment answers instead. Any object with a get(key) method works as the store, including a plain dict, which is how a caller supplies tokens without a keychain. An empty dict counts as no store, and the default EnvStore is used:

infra = Infra(env={'HCLOUD_TOKEN': 'hc-demo'})
infra.token('HCLOUD_TOKEN'), infra.token('CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN')

('hc-demo', '')


status reports which libraries are installed and which tokens are set, without revealing the values and without sending a request:

Infra(env={'HCLOUD_TOKEN': 'hc-demo'}).status()

{'vpseasy': True,
 'cfeasy': True,
 'hcloud_token': True,
 'cf_token': False,
 'keys': ['HCLOUD_TOKEN', 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN']}


The listing methods return trimmed rows: servers and keys (the account’s SSH keys) from Hetzner, and tunnels, zones and records from Cloudflare. tunnels leaves out deleted tunnels, and records takes a zone’s name or its 32-character id. verify runs cfeasy’s token check, so a missing permission shows up before a deploy runs into it. delete_server and delete_tunnel remove one resource each, and delete_server first checks that a server of that name exists.
Both deletions check their argument before anything else, so an empty name fails without a request:

test_fail(lambda: Infra(env={'HCLOUD_TOKEN': 'hc-demo'}).delete_server(' '), contains='name the server')
test_fail(lambda: Infra(env={'HCLOUD_TOKEN': 'hc-demo'}).delete_tunnel(''), contains='name the tunnel')

overview fetches servers, tunnels and zones in one call. Each section is {rows, error}, so a Cloudflare failure cannot hide the servers. An InfraError appears as its message alone, and any other exception with its type name in front:

o = Infra(env={'HCLOUD_TOKEN': '', 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN': ''}).overview()
o['zones']

{'rows': [],
 'error': 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN is not set — add it in Workflows → Environment'}

title: pipeline
text:
A pipeline is an ordered plan of commands for one project, together with the record of how each one went. pullup’s release, deploy and drive features are all pipelines. This module runs the commands one at a time, each in its own pseudo-terminal (PTY), copies their output into one transcript that any number of viewers can follow, and keeps the plan in a JSON file inside the project so it survives a restart.


source

PipelineError
def PipelineError(
    *args, **kwargs
):
Unspecified run-time error.


PipelineError is the only exception this module raises: for an unknown step id, a plan with nothing to run, or a request to start a step while another is running. A step that exits with a non-zero code does not raise. It is a result: the step is marked failed, its exit code is kept, and state reports both.


source

uv_argv
def uv_argv(
    root, argv
):
The command wrapped in uv run for a project with a uv.lock, or None when uv does not apply.




source

resolve_script
def resolve_script(
    argv, python:NoneType=None, env:NoneType=None
):
The command with its program replaced by a full path, trying both the hyphen and the underscore spelling.


Before running a command the pipeline has to find the program. Python tools get installed under either spelling of their name, so nbdev_prepare may be on disk as nbdev-prepare. resolve_script tries the name as given and with underscores and hyphens swapped, first in the directory of the chosen interpreter and then on PATH, and puts the full path in place of the name. A command it cannot find comes back unchanged, so the error names the program you asked for.
uv_argv handles projects managed by uv. When the project has a uv.lock and uv is installed, it returns the command wrapped in uv run --project <root>, using whichever spelling exists in the project’s .venv/bin. Otherwise it returns None and the pipeline falls back to resolve_script.

argv = resolve_script(['my-tool', '--flag'], python=bindir/'python')
Path(argv[0]).name, argv[1:], resolve_script(['not-installed-anywhere'])

('my_tool', ['--flag'], ['not-installed-anywhere'])



(root/'uv.lock').write_text('')
argv = uv_argv(root, ['my-tool', '-q'])
argv[0], argv[3] = Path(argv[0]).name, '<project>'
argv

['uv', 'run', '--project', '<project>', 'my_tool', '-q']




source

Pipeline
def Pipeline(
    root, # the project the commands run in
    python:NoneType=None, # the interpreter whose virtual environment they run in; None uses this process's
    env:NoneType=None, # an `EnvStore`, or anything with `.get(key)` and `.values(keys)`
    dir:str='.pullup', # where the plan is written, relative to `root`
):
An ordered plan of commands for one project, with each step’s result and a shared terminal transcript.


Pipeline is the class the rest of pullup builds on. You give it a project folder and, if you like, the interpreter whose virtual environment the commands should use (python), an environment store for the keys steps need (env), and the directory for the plan (dir).
save takes a list of step dictionaries and writes them to <root>/<dir>/pipeline.json. Each row needs a cmd. Rows without one are dropped, and a plan with no rows left raises. Missing ids become step1, step2 and so on. When the file is missing, unreadable or empty, the pipeline uses its class’s defaults, which for the base class is an empty plan.
state returns everything a caller needs to draw the pipeline: each step with its status (pending, running, passed, failed or skipped), its exit code and the keys it is missing, plus whether the whole plan is done.

p = Pipeline(proj, dir='.demo')
st = p.save([{'label': 'say hello', 'cmd': 'echo hello from a pipeline'},
             {'id': 'ok', 'label': 'exit clean', 'cmd': 'true'},
             {'label': 'no command of its own'}])
[(r['id'], r['label'], r['status']) for r in st['steps']]

[('step1', 'say hello', 'pending'), ('ok', 'exit clean', 'pending')]


start runs one step: the one you name, or else the first that has not passed or been skipped. With auto=True, the default, each step that passes starts the next, and the first failure ends the run. start returns once the step has been launched, so the example waits for the run to settle before reading the state. tail then returns the end of the transcript as plain text, with colour codes removed.

await p.start()
st = await settle(p)
[(r['id'], r['status'], r['code']) for r in st['steps']]

[('step1', 'passed', 0), ('ok', 'passed', 0)]



print(p.tail(9))


❯ echo hello from a pipeline
hello from a pipeline

✓ say hello exited 0

❯ true

✓ exit clean exited 0


A failing step leaves every step after it pending, and its exit code is the child process’s own. To carry on, fix the cause and call start again, which picks up at the failed step, or skip it.

q = Pipeline(proj, dir='.fail')
q.save([{'id': 'tests', 'label': 'tests', 'cmd': 'sh -c "exit 3"'},
        {'id': 'publish', 'label': 'publish', 'cmd': 'echo publishing'}])
await q.start()
[(r['id'], r['status'], r['code']) for r in (await settle(q))['steps']]

[('tests', 'failed', 3), ('publish', 'pending', None)]


A user interface usually shows the transcript live. subscribe returns an asyncio.Queue that first holds everything already in the transcript and then receives each new chunk of output as it arrives. unsubscribe stops the updates. write sends keystrokes to the running step, for example when twine asks for a password, and resize changes the size of its terminal.

sub = p.subscribe()
b'hello from a pipeline' in sub.get_nowait()

True


needs lists every environment key the plan names, once each, in the order the steps name them. missing lists the keys one step needs that the store cannot supply, so a user interface can ask for them before the step runs and fails.

r = Pipeline(proj, dir='.needs', env=Store(GITHUB_TOKEN='ghp_pretend'))
r.save([{'id': 'gh', 'label': 'GitHub release', 'cmd': 'true', 'needs': ['GITHUB_TOKEN']},
        {'id': 'pypi', 'label': 'PyPI', 'cmd': 'true', 'needs': ['TWINE_PASSWORD', 'GITHUB_TOKEN']}])
r.needs(), [(s.id, r.missing(s)) for s in r.steps]

(['GITHUB_TOKEN', 'TWINE_PASSWORD'],
 [('gh', []), ('pypi', ['TWINE_PASSWORD'])])


The remaining controls change the results, never the saved plan. skip marks a step done without running it. stop kills the running step, marks it failed and turns off automatic continuation. reset forgets every result and clears the transcript, so the plan can run again from the top. reset_plan puts the default plan back in memory and leaves the saved file alone. After a failure, blame reads the transcript to name which of your packages raised (see the stack module); it returns {} when nothing has failed.


source

Release
def Release(
    root, # the project the commands run in
    python:NoneType=None, # the interpreter whose virtual environment they run in; None uses this process's
    env:NoneType=None, # an `EnvStore`, or anything with `.get(key)` and `.values(keys)`
    dir:str='.pullup', # where the plan is written, relative to `root`
):
The release pipeline, whose default plan is the project’s release flow.


Release is the pipeline for publishing a package. Its default plan is the project’s release flow from default_steps, it saves to release.json, and its state also reports the flow’s name and whether the project is nbdev, fastship, or builds a desktop app.

rl = Release(rroot)
rl.state()['flow'], [s.id for s in rl.steps], rl.path.name

('nbdev', ['prepare', 'bump', 'gh', 'pypi'], 'release.json')

title: stack
text:
When a release fails, the traceback often runs through several of your own packages, sometimes through installed copies of them rather than the checkouts you edit. This module answers three questions: which of your packages are installed, where an import of each one resolves to, and which one raised an error.
Nothing here imports the packages it reports on. Every answer comes from import metadata, a file path, or the text of a traceback, so a package that fails to import can still be described.
FAMILY is the default list of your own packages: the ones pullup is built from, and the only ones a report blames. A frame in json or asyncio is someone else’s code and is passed over. Every function that takes family= uses your list instead, and an empty family means FAMILY.


source

installed
def installed(
    name
):
Whether name is importable, without importing it.


installed says whether Python can find the module, without importing it. A module that is found but fails when imported still counts as installed.

installed('nbdev'), installed('no_such_package_here'), installed('')

(True, False, False)




source

checkout_for
def checkout_for(
    name, checkouts
):
The folder in checkouts that holds package name, found by its __init__.py rather than the folder name.




source

survey
def survey(
    family:tuple=(), checkouts:tuple=()
):
One row per family package: installed, version, the copy an import resolves to, and whether a checkout is shadowed.


survey describes each package in the family in one row: whether it is installed, its version, and the path an import resolves to. source is checkout when that path is a working tree and site-packages when it is inside an installed environment, and editable is true in the first case. Pass the folders you work in as checkouts, and checkout names the one that holds the package. shadowed is true when you have a checkout of a package but Python imports an installed copy instead, so your edits have no effect:

[{k: r[k] for k in ('name', 'installed', 'source', 'shadowed')}
 for r in survey(family=['pullup', 'nbdev', 'dhrishti'])]

[{'name': 'pullup',
  'installed': True,
  'source': 'checkout',
  'shadowed': False},
 {'name': 'nbdev',
  'installed': True,
  'source': 'site-packages',
  'shadowed': False},
 {'name': 'dhrishti', 'installed': False, 'source': '', 'shadowed': False}]


The checkout is matched by what is inside it rather than by its folder name, so a fork called nbdev-fork still holds the nbdev package and is still the checkout for it.

fork = root/'nbdev-fork'; (fork/'nbdev').mkdir(parents=True)
(fork/'nbdev'/'__init__.py').write_text('')
row = survey(family=['nbdev'], checkouts=[fork])[0]
{k: row[k] for k in ('source', 'editable', 'shadowed')}

{'source': 'site-packages', 'editable': False, 'shadowed': True}




source

frames
def frames(
    text
):
Every File ..., line N, in f in a traceback, oldest first, as the terminal printed it.


frames pulls every File "...", line N, in f line out of a traceback’s text, oldest first, as the terminal printed them. Text without frames gives an empty list. The example builds a small package that raises:

pkg = root/'blowup'; pkg.mkdir()
(pkg/'__init__.py').write_text('')
(pkg/'core.py').write_text("""def push(remote):
    raise RuntimeError(f"no upstream for {remote}")

def sync():
    push("origin")
""")
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))


from blowup.core import sync
try: sync()
except RuntimeError: tb = traceback.format_exc()
print(tb.replace(str(root), '/proj'))

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<ipython-input-23-1bc83a927e6d>", line 2, in <module>
    try: sync()
         ^^^^^^
  File "/proj/blowup/core.py", line 5, in sync
    push("origin")
  File "/proj/blowup/core.py", line 2, in push
    raise RuntimeError(f"no upstream for {remote}")
RuntimeError: no upstream for origin



The deepest frame is the one that ran the raise, and it is the last one frames returns.

{**frames(tb)[-1], 'file': frames(tb)[-1]['file'].replace(str(root), '/proj')}

{'file': '/proj/blowup/core.py', 'line': 2, 'fn': 'push'}


_package_of names the family package a file belongs to. For a file under site-packages it is the folder directly below site-packages, so a copy vendored inside another package is not blamed. For any other path it is the last folder whose name is in the family:

(_package_of('/home/me/code/gheasy/gheasy/repo.py', ['gheasy']),
 _package_of('/x/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/vendorpkg/gheasy/repo.py', ['gheasy']),
 _package_of('/usr/lib/python3.11/json/decoder.py', ['gheasy']))

('gheasy', '', '')


_is_error picks out the line that names the exception, such as RuntimeError: no upstream for origin or a bare RuntimeError, and rejects the header, the frame lines and echoed source lines. blame reads the traceback from the bottom and takes the first line it accepts:

[_is_error(l) for l in ('Traceback (most recent call last):',
                        '  File "core.py", line 2, in push',
                        '    if not upstream:',
                        'RuntimeError',
                        'RuntimeError: no upstream for origin')]

[False, False, False, True, True]




source

blame
def blame(
    text, checkouts:tuple=(), family:NoneType=None
):
Which family package raised, from the deepest family frame, and the file to open, preferring your checkout.


blame puts these together. It finds the deepest frame that belongs to a family package, takes the error line, and returns the package, file, line, function, error, installed version and checkout. open is the file to open in an editor. When no frame belongs to the family, package is empty but error is still filled in:

r = blame(tb, checkouts=[root], family=['blowup'])
{k: (v.replace(str(root), '/proj') if isinstance(v, str) else v) for k, v in r.items()}

{'package': 'blowup',
 'file': '/proj/blowup/core.py',
 'line': 2,
 'fn': 'push',
 'error': 'RuntimeError: no upstream for origin',
 'open': '/proj/blowup/core.py',
 'checkout': '/proj',
 'version': ''}


The traceback names the copy that ran. When you pass checkouts and that copy was installed rather than checked out, open points at the same file in your checkout, which is the copy you can edit:

other = root/'blowup-fork'; (other/'blowup').mkdir(parents=True)
(other/'blowup'/'__init__.py').write_text(''); (other/'blowup'/'core.py').write_text('')
moved = blame(tb, checkouts=[other], family=['blowup'])
moved['file'] == moved['open'], moved['open'].startswith(str(other))

(False, True)


An exception raised with no message still has an error line, and it is the class name alone.
In a chained traceback, error is the last exception raised and the frame is the deepest family frame anywhere in the text. Those two are not always parts of the same exception.

title: pullup
text:
pullup is the engine behind a release and deploy panel. Point it at a project folder and it tells you what kind of project it is (an nbdev library, a plain Python package, a Rust crate and so on) and which commands release it. It then runs those commands in a terminal you can watch, and stops at the first one that fails. The same machinery runs the deploy of a web app to a virtual private server (VPS). pullup also reads the GitHub Actions workflows in the repository, writes new ones, and lists the Hetzner servers and Cloudflare tunnels the project uses.
Every public call returns plain dictionaries and lists, so a user interface can draw them and a test can compare them. The work that talks to GitHub, Docker, Hetzner and Cloudflare is done by four sibling libraries: gheasy, dockeasy, vpseasy and cfeasy.

title: pullup
text:
Install
pip install pullup
This also installs gheasy, dockeasy, vpseasy and cfeasy. None of them is imported until a call needs it, so reading a project or running a release does not load them.

title: pullup
section: What kind of project is this
text:
What kind of project is this
A release flow is the ordered list of commands that publishes one kind of project. An nbdev library is released with nbdev-prepare, nbdev-bump-version, nbdev-release-gh and nbdev-pypi. A plain Python package and a Rust crate each have a different list. Project looks at the files in a folder, picks the flow that fits, and returns its steps. The folder here holds only a pyproject.toml with a [tool.nbdev] table, so it is an nbdev project:

project = Project(root)
project.kind, [step.id for step in project.steps()]

('nbdev', ['prepare', 'bump', 'gh', 'pypi'])

title: pullup
text:
Running the steps
A Pipeline runs a list of steps for one project. Each step runs in a pseudo-terminal (PTY), so a program that asks for a password behaves as it would in your own shell, and every step’s output goes into one shared transcript. When a step passes, the next one starts by itself. When one fails, the pipeline stops there.
save stores the plan and start launches the first step that has not yet passed. start returns as soon as the step is running, not when it finishes, which is why the transcript below shows the command but not yet its output. Call state or tail whenever you want to see how far it has got.

pipeline = Pipeline(root, dir='.demo')
pipeline.save([{'id': 'hello', 'cmd': 'say hello',
                'argv': [sys.executable, '-c', 'print("ready")']}])
await pipeline.start()
pipeline.state()['done'], pipeline.tail().splitlines()[-2:]

(False, ['', '❯ say hello'])

title: pullup
text:
Where plans are kept
A saved plan is a JSON file inside the project folder, in the directory you pass as dir (.pullup unless you say otherwise). pullup never writes a plan outside the project:

custom = Pipeline(root, dir='.myapp')
custom.save([{'id': 'show', 'cmd': 'show', 'argv': [sys.executable, '-c', 'print("saved")']}])
custom.path.relative_to(root)

Path('.myapp/pipeline.json')

title: pullup
text:
Deploying a web app
Deploy is a pipeline that puts a web app on a server. Its steps run the subcommands of a deploy.py script that lives in the project, and Deploy.scaffold can write that script for you. Drive covers the same ground one library call at a time (write the Dockerfile, open the tunnel, provision the server), so you can run and check each part on its own. Both are pipelines, so they start, stop and report like the one above.

Deploy(root).state()['kind'], Drive(root).state()['kind']

('deploy', 'drive')

title: pullup
text:
Workflows
Workflows reads the GitHub Actions files in .github/workflows and turns each one into a row of triggers and jobs. Reading local files needs no GitHub token. Listing runs, starting them and pushing secrets do.

workflow_dir = root/'.github'/'workflows'
workflow_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
(workflow_dir/'ci.yml').write_text('''name: CI
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: pytest
''')
workflows = Workflows(root)
[(row['name'], [job['id'] for job in row['jobs']]) for row in workflows.parsed()]

[('CI', ['test'])]

title: pullup
text:
Environment values
Many steps need a token or a setting, such as GITHUB_TOKEN for a GitHub release. A step lists the names it needs under needs, and the pipeline looks them up in an environment store when it starts the step. The values are given to the child process only, and your own process environment is left alone. The default store is an EnvStore, which keeps secrets in the system keychain, but any object with get and values methods will do, like the small one below:

class Values:
    def get(self, key, secret=True): return 'demo-token' if key == 'DEMO_TOKEN' else ''
    def values(self, keys): return {key: self.get(key) for key in keys if self.get(key)}

with_values = Pipeline(root, env=Values(), dir='.env-demo')
with_values.save([{'id': 'env', 'cmd': 'read environment', 'needs': ['DEMO_TOKEN'],
                   'argv': [sys.executable, '-c', 'import os; print(os.environ["DEMO_TOKEN"])']}])
await with_values.start()
with_values.tail().splitlines()[-2:]

['', '❯ read environment']

title: pullup
text:
Which package broke
When a step fails with a Python traceback, the useful question is which of your own packages raised it. blame reads the traceback text, finds the deepest frame that belongs to one of the packages named in family, and returns that package with the file, the line, the function and the error message:

trace = '''Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/tmp/pullup/demo.py", line 7, in release
    raise RuntimeError("stopped")
RuntimeError: stopped
'''
blame(trace, family=['pullup'])

{'package': 'pullup',
 'file': '/tmp/pullup/demo.py',
 'line': 7,
 'fn': 'release',
 'error': 'RuntimeError: stopped',
 'open': '/tmp/pullup/demo.py',
 'checkout': '',
 'version': '0.0.4'}

title: pullup
text:
Servers and tunnels
Infra lists and deletes Hetzner servers and Cloudflare tunnels, and lists Cloudflare zones and DNS records, using the tokens in the project’s environment store. status says which of the two libraries are installed and which tokens are set, without sending a request. An empty env falls back to the default EnvStore, so the answer below reflects the keychain of the machine that ran it:

infra = Infra(env={})
infra.status()

{'vpseasy': True,
 'cfeasy': True,
 'hcloud_token': True,
 'cf_token': False,
 'keys': ['HCLOUD_TOKEN', 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN']}

title: deploy
text:
This module puts a web app on a virtual private server (VPS). It follows the pattern of lego, the project it was taken from: a Docker image described by dockeasy, a Hetzner server provisioned by vpseasy, and a Cloudflare tunnel opened by cfeasy, so the app is reachable without opening a public port. The work is done by two scripts in the project, setup.py for one-time setup and deploy.py for every deploy. This module writes both, and Deploy is the pipeline that runs deploy.py.


source

generator
def generator():
The tool name that generated scripts say wrote them.




source

use_generator
def use_generator(
    name
):
Set the tool name that generated setup.py and deploy.py files say wrote them.


Each generated script says in its docstring which tool wrote it. use_generator sets that name, which is Leela until you change it. A host application that bundles pullup calls it with its own name. The templates read the name each time they build their text, so a call made after import still takes effect.
DeployError is another name for PipelineError, so catching either one catches both.
DEPLOY_KEYS lists the settings a deploy needs. A value of None marks a secret: it has no default and goes to GitHub as an encrypted secret. A string marks an ordinary variable, and the string is its default. MODE, PORT, SERVER_USER and RSYNC_FORCE have defaults; the domain, the server name and the three tokens do not.

{k: ('secret' if v is None else f'variable, default {v!r}') for k, v in DEPLOY_KEYS.items()}

{'MODE': "variable, default 'prod'",
 'PORT': "variable, default '5001'",
 'DOMAIN': 'secret',
 'SERVER_NAME': 'secret',
 'SERVER_USER': "variable, default 'deploy'",
 'HCLOUD_TOKEN': 'secret',
 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN': 'secret',
 'CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN': 'secret',
 'RSYNC_FORCE': "variable, default 'false'"}


DEPLOY_STEPS is the default deploy plan. Each step runs one subcommand of the project’s deploy.py. env writes the .env file the container reads. compose writes the Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml and the Caddyfile. deploy opens the tunnel, provisions the server if it does not exist yet and copies the project to it with rsync. Only the last step needs tokens.

[(s.id, s.cmd, s.needs) for s in DEPLOY_STEPS]

[('env', 'python deploy.py env', []),
 ('compose', 'python deploy.py compose', []),
 ('deploy',
  'python deploy.py deploy',
  ['HCLOUD_TOKEN', 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN'])]




source

setup_template
def setup_template(
    app, domain, subdomain:str='', port:int=5001, lfs:bool=True
):
The text of a one-time setup.py that prepares a project for deploying the lego way.


setup_template returns the text of a setup.py for the project, without writing it. Run once after scaffolding, that script records the keys in gheasy’s config, tracks images and audio with Git LFS, writes .env.example with an empty value for each secret, writes the GitHub deploy workflow, and copies each installed library’s SKILL.md for coding agents. Its subcommands push your local values to GitHub (push), leaving out keys with no value so a secret is never set to the text None, upload the server’s SSH key as the DEPLOY_KEY secret (ssh-key), and redo single parts (mkenv, workflow, skills).
ENV_KEYS in the generated file lists every key the script handles, with the domain filled in. It is DEPLOY_KEYS plus SERVER_PASSWORD:

src = setup_template('lego', 'example.com', subdomain='app')
literal(src, 'ENV_KEYS')

{'MODE': 'prod',
 'PORT': 5001,
 'DOMAIN': 'app.example.com',
 'SERVER_NAME': None,
 'SERVER_USER': 'deploy',
 'SERVER_PASSWORD': None,
 'HCLOUD_TOKEN': None,
 'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN': None,
 'CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN': None,
 'RSYNC_FORCE': 'false'}




source

deploy_template
def deploy_template(
    app, domain, subdomain:str='', port:int=5001, second_host:str=''
):
The text of a deploy.py that builds, tunnels and deploys the app; second_host adds another hostname.


deploy_template returns the text of the deploy.py itself. Its subcommands are env, compose and deploy, which the pipeline’s steps call, plus status, which lists the servers and tunnels your tokens can see, rollback, which runs the image from before the last deploy or a kept image you name, and nuke, which deletes the server once you type back a random confirmation word. nuke keeps the Cloudflare tunnel unless you add --tunnel, because the tunnel follows whichever server runs its connector and survives a move to a new box. After a deploy, after_deploy waits until the site answers and purges Cloudflare’s cache for the host; vpseasy’s deploy has already kept the replaced image for rollback and pruned dangling images. The tunnel is named <subdomain or app>_<domain>. second_host adds another hostname served by the same tunnel and container. The file is meant to be edited, and the pipeline runs whatever it says.

dsrc = deploy_template('lego', 'example.com', subdomain='app')
literal(dsrc, 'host'), literal(dsrc, 'tunnel_name'), literal(dsrc, 'inc')[:4]

('app.example.com',
 'app_example.com',
 ['lego/', 'static/', 'pyproject.toml', 'uv.lock'])




source

Deploy
def Deploy(
    root, # the project the commands run in
    python:NoneType=None, # the interpreter whose virtual environment they run in; None uses this process's
    env:NoneType=None, # an `EnvStore`, or anything with `.get(key)` and `.values(keys)`
    dir:str='.pullup', # where the plan is written, relative to `root`
):
The deploy pipeline, one step per subcommand of the project’s deploy.py.


Deploy is the pipeline for all of this. Its default plan is DEPLOY_STEPS, saved to deploy.json in the plan directory.
scaffold sets a project up for deploying. It writes deploy.py, writes setup.py if there is none, adds the deploy keys to .gheasy/config.json, and adds the deploy workflow through Workflows. It needs a domain, and it refuses to replace an existing deploy.py unless you pass force=True. It returns the paths it wrote along with the new state:

d = Deploy(root)
[str(Path(p).relative_to(root)) for p in d.scaffold(domain='example.com', subdomain='app')['written']]

['deploy.py',
 'setup.py',
 '.gheasy/config.json',
 '.github/workflows/deploy.yml']


target reports where the deploy goes and what is still missing, read from the same store the steps will use: the app, domain, server, user and port, the secret keys with no value yet, and which of the generated files exist. A user interface can tell from it whether a project has been scaffolded and what to ask for before the first deploy, and state includes it under target. Each key is also read in lower case, such as server_name, for projects whose .env and GitHub variables predate the upper-case names. The values come from the default store, so they reflect the machine that ran this page.

{k: v for k, v in d.target().items() if k != 'keys'}

{'app': 'lego',
 'domain': 'app.example.com',
 'server': '',
 'user': 'deploy',
 'port': '5001',
 'missing': ['SERVER_NAME',
  'HCLOUD_TOKEN',
  'CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN',
  'CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN'],
 'script': True,
 'setup': True,
 'compose': False,
 'dockerfile': False,
 'caddyfile': False}

title: drive
text:
Deploy runs the whole deploy through one script. When something goes wrong halfway, it helps to run the parts separately and see what each one printed. Drive is a pipeline whose steps are six short Python snippets, each calling one library function: write the Dockerfile, write the compose stack, open the tunnel, point an extra hostname at it, provision the server, and push the secrets to GitHub. You can read each snippet, run it, fix the cause of a failure and run it again.
Drive saves its plan to drive.json, apart from the Deploy plan, so neither overwrites the other. DriveError is the same class as PipelineError.

DRIVE_FILE, DriveError is PipelineError

('drive.json', True)




source

Part
def Part(
    id:str, package:str, label:str, doc:str, code:str, needs:list=<factory>, writes:list=<factory>,
    produces:list=<factory>
)->None:
One deploy operation as a code template that can run as a step on its own.


A part is one deploy operation written as a code template. Part holds the package the code calls, a label and description for display, the code with {placeholders} for the project’s values, the keys the code reads (needs), the keys it stores (writes), and the files it creates (produces).
PARTS holds the six parts in the order they run. image writes the Dockerfile that dockeasy detects. stack wraps that image in a compose file with Caddy and cloudflared. tunnel creates or reuses the Cloudflare tunnel and stores its token. dns points SECOND_HOST at the same tunnel, and stops with a message when that key is unset. server provisions the Hetzner server if it is missing, copies the project over and starts the stack. secrets pushes the declared keys to GitHub so that CI can run the same deploy.

for p in PARTS: print(f'{p.id:8} {p.package:9} {p.label:18} needs={p.needs} writes={p.writes}')

image    dockeasy  Dockerfile         needs=[] writes=[]
stack    vpseasy   compose stack      needs=[] writes=[]
tunnel   cfeasy    Cloudflare tunnel  needs=['CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN'] writes=['CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN']
dns      cfeasy    extra hostname     needs=['CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN'] writes=[]
server   vpseasy   server and rsync   needs=['HCLOUD_TOKEN'] writes=['HETZNER_IP']
secrets  gheasy    push secrets       needs=['GITHUB_TOKEN'] writes=[]




source

context
def context(
    root, env:NoneType=None
):
The project values every part’s template is filled with: names, host, tunnel, port and file lists.


context works out, once, every value the templates use. The app name comes from gheasy’s config, then the name in pyproject.toml, then the folder name. DOMAIN from the store is split into a subdomain and a base domain when it has more than one dot, and the tunnel name follows the same rule as in deploy.py. keys lists the keys in gheasy’s env_schema, or just DOMAIN when there is none.

ctx = context(root, env)
{k: ctx[k] for k in ('app', 'host', 'domain', 'subdomain', 'tunnel', 'port', 'keys')}

{'app': 'demo',
 'host': 'app.example.com',
 'domain': 'example.com',
 'subdomain': 'app',
 'tunnel': 'app_example.com',
 'port': '8080',
 'keys': ['DOMAIN']}


_step fills a part’s template from the context and wraps it in a Step whose argv runs the code with python -c. The filled-in code is also kept in meta['code'], so a user interface can show exactly what will run. This is the tunnel part for the example project:

s = _step(PARTS[2], 'python', ctx)
print(s.label, '|', s.cmd, '|', s.needs)
print(s.meta['code'])

cfeasy · Cloudflare tunnel | python -c … cfeasy | ['CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN']
from cfeasy import CF
from dockeasy import env_get, env_set
cf = CF(token=env_get('CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN'))
tid, tok = cf.setup_tunnel('example.com', 'app' or None, tunnel_name='app_example.com')
env_set('CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN', tok)
print('tunnel', tid, 'for', 'app.example.com')




source

parts
def parts(
    root, env:NoneType=None, python:str=''
):
Every part as a runnable Step, its template filled with this project’s values.


parts does the same for all six parts, with one context and the interpreter you choose (this process’s Python by default). This is the last one, which pushes the secrets:

steps = parts(root, env)
test_eq(steps[0].argv[0], sys.executable)
print(steps[-1].meta['code'].replace(str(root), '/proj'))

from gheasy import gh_push_env
from dockeasy import env_get
keys = ['DOMAIN']
vals = {k: v for k in keys if (v := env_get(k, default=''))}
print('pushing', len(vals), 'of', len(keys), 'declared keys')
gh_push_env(vals, path='/proj')




source

Drive
def Drive(
    root, python:NoneType=None, env:NoneType=None, dir:str='.pullup'
):
The deploy as six separate library calls, each a step you can run on its own.


Drive uses these rendered parts as its default plan. Until you save a plan, refresh (which state calls) renders the parts again whenever the values in the store change, so changing DOMAIN changes the snippets. Once a plan is saved it is used as written. state also returns the context and the four packages involved.

d = Drive(root, env=env)
st = d.state()
[r['id'] for r in st['steps']], st['packages'], st['needs'], st['configured']

(['image', 'stack', 'tunnel', 'dns', 'server', 'secrets'],
 ['cfeasy', 'dockeasy', 'gheasy', 'vpseasy'],
 ['CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN', 'HCLOUD_TOKEN', 'GITHUB_TOKEN'],
 False)

title: workflows
text:
GitHub Actions runs the YAML files in a repository’s .github/workflows folder. Each file is a workflow: it says which events start it (on) and which jobs to run, and a job can wait for others through needs. This module reads those files into rows a user interface can draw, talks to GitHub about runs and secrets through gheasy, and writes new workflows from gheasy’s recipes.


source

WorkflowError
def WorkflowError(
    *args, **kwargs
):
Unspecified run-time error.


WorkflowError is the only exception this module raises. Reading local files never raises it: parse puts the reason on the row’s error and returns the row. Writing a file, calling GitHub without gheasy or a token, starting a run and pushing a secret do raise it.


source

gheasy_core
def gheasy_core():
Return the gheasy.core module, raising WorkflowError with the install hint when gheasy is missing.


gheasy_core imports gheasy for every function that needs it, and is public for hosts that drive the same module; _gheasy remains as an alias. When gheasy is missing, the call fails with a WorkflowError that names the install command. _opened finds a gheasy helper under its public name or under the underscored name that older gheasy releases used.


source

levels
def levels(
    jobs
):
Arrange jobs into rows, each one row below its deepest dependency, with any cycle in a last row.


PyYAML follows YAML 1.1, which reads the bare key on as the boolean True, so a workflow’s triggers end up under the wrong key. _yaml uses gheasy’s YAML 1.2 parser when gheasy is installed, which keeps on as a string, and otherwise wraps PyYAML. parse accepts both. The example shows the two parsers side by side:

list(_yaml().load('on: push')), list(yaml.safe_load('on: push'))

(['on'], [True])


levels arranges jobs into rows for drawing a graph. Jobs with no dependencies go in the first row, and every other job goes one row below its deepest dependency. A needs entry that names a job not in the list is ignored. Jobs caught in a dependency cycle cannot be placed this way, so they all go together in one last row instead of raising an error.

jobs = [{'id': 'lint', 'needs': []}, {'id': 'test', 'needs': []},
        {'id': 'ship', 'needs': ['lint', 'test']}, {'id': 'notify', 'needs': ['ship']}]
levels(jobs)

[['lint', 'test'], ['ship'], ['notify']]




source

Workflows
def Workflows(
    root
):
The workflows of one repository: local files, runs on GitHub, the catalogue, and secrets.


Workflows covers one repository: its local workflow files, their runs on GitHub, the catalogue of workflows pullup can add, and the secrets and variables those workflows read. The examples use this workflow, which has three triggers and a ship job that waits for lint and test:

WF = r'''name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 4 * * 1'
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ruff check .
  test:
    name: pytest
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: run the suite
        run: |
          uv sync
          pytest -q
  ship:
    needs: [lint, test]
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment: pypi
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo ship
'''

files returns the .yml and .yaml files in .github/workflows, sorted by name. Other files in the folder are ignored, as GitHub ignores them. A repository without the folder gives [], not an error.

w = Workflows(repo)
[p.name for p in w.files()]

['ci.yml', 'docs.yml']


parse turns one file into a row: the workflow’s name, its triggers, its jobs, their levels, and whether it can be started by hand (dispatchable, true when it declares workflow_dispatch). A file that cannot be read or is not valid YAML still gives a row, with the reason in error. parsed does this for every file:

row = w.parse(wfs/'ci.yml')
row['name'], row['dispatchable'], row['levels']

('CI', True, [['lint', 'test'], ['ship']])



[(r['name'], r['dispatchable'], r['error']) for r in w.parsed()]

[('CI', True, ''), ('Docs', True, '')]


_triggers turns the on block into a list of event and detail rows. GitHub allows three shapes for on: a single event name, a list of names, or a mapping from each event to its filters, such as branches or a cron schedule. All three come out in the same form:

row['triggers']

[{'event': 'push', 'detail': 'branches: main'},
 {'event': 'schedule', 'detail': '0 4 * * 1'},
 {'event': 'workflow_dispatch', 'detail': ''}]


_job turns one entry under jobs into a row. needs may be one name or a list, and environment may be a name or a mapping with a name; both come out in one form. Each step is labelled by its name, or else its uses, or else the first line of its run:

[(j['id'], j['name'], j['needs'], j['environment']) for j in row['jobs']]

[('lint', 'lint', [], ''),
 ('test', 'pytest', [], ''),
 ('ship', 'ship', ['lint', 'test'], 'pypi')]



[(s['name'], s['uses']) for s in row['jobs'][1]['steps']]

[('actions/checkout@v4', 'actions/checkout@v4'), ('run the suite', '')]


Everything so far reads local files and uses no network. The methods that follow call GitHub through gheasy and need a token in GITHUB_TOKEN. status says which of gheasy, a GitHub remote and the token is missing. runs lists recent runs, run_jobs lists the jobs and steps of one run, dispatch starts a workflow that declares workflow_dispatch, and cancel stops a run. remote_env lists the secrets and variables already on GitHub; GitHub returns only the names of secrets, never their values.
_fastship loads gheasy’s fastship release recipe, which gheasy gained in 0.0.8. With an older gheasy it raises WorkflowError asking you to upgrade.
_gh_authed runs gh auth status, the only way to find out whether the GitHub CLI is logged in. A missing gh, a timeout or a non-zero exit all count as not logged in.
_wf_name is the check every write goes through. A name with a directory in it, or with any suffix other than .yml or .yaml, is refused. Nothing outside .github/workflows is written by this module.

test_fail(lambda: _wf_name('.github/workflows/ci.yml'), contains='not a workflow file name')
test_fail(lambda: _wf_name('Makefile'), contains='not a workflow file name')
test_eq(_wf_name('ci.yaml'), 'ci.yaml')
test_eq(_from_line('# built by dockeasy\nFROM python:3.12-slim\nRUN uv sync'), 'FROM python:3.12-slim')
test_eq(_from_line(''), '')
test_eq(_read(repo/'nowhere.toml'), '')

_run_row turns one run from GitHub’s API into a flat row for display. The title is the run’s display title, or else the first line of the head commit’s message:

run = {'id': 178, 'name': 'CI', 'path': '.github/workflows/ci.yml', 'run_number': 12,
       'status': 'completed', 'conclusion': 'failure', 'head_branch': 'main', 'event': 'push',
       'html_url': 'https://github.com/o/r/actions/runs/178', 'actor': {'login': 'jph'},
       'head_commit': {'message': 'drop the retry\n\nit never fired'}}
_run_row(run)

{'id': 178,
 'name': 'CI',
 'file': 'ci.yml',
 'number': 12,
 'status': 'completed',
 'conclusion': 'failure',
 'branch': 'main',
 'event': 'push',
 'created_at': '',
 'updated_at': '',
 'url': 'https://github.com/o/r/actions/runs/178',
 'actor': 'jph',
 'title': 'drop the retry'}


detect describes the project from its working tree. Each flag is true when a file exists or a name appears in pyproject.toml or requirements.txt: web looks for FastHTML, FastAPI, Django or Flask, vps for vpseasy, cfeasy or hcloud, and publish for a build backend. build is the FROM line of the Dockerfile dockeasy would write, and build_why says why it is empty: dockeasy is missing, or its detect_app raised.

(repo/'pyproject.toml').write_text('[project]\nname = "demo"\ndependencies = ["python-fasthtml"]\n'
                                   '[build-system]\nrequires = ["hatchling"]\n')
det = w.detect()
{k: v for k, v in det.items() if v}

{'python': True,
 'fastship': True,
 'web': True,
 'publish': True,
 'build': 'FROM ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.13-bookworm AS builder'}


catalogue lists the seven workflows pullup can add, all built from gheasy’s recipes. For each one it says whether this project wants it (recommended, with the reason in why) and whether a file of that name already exists (present). The example project is a FastHTML package built with hatchling, so Python CI, a fastship release and a Docker image are recommended. Both CI entries show as present because they write ci.yml, which the example repository already has:

[(r['id'], r['recommended'], r['present'], r['why']) for r in w.catalogue()['workflows']]

[('ci', True, True, 'a Python project'),
 ('nbdev', False, True, ''),
 ('pypi', False, False, ''),
 ('fastship', True, False, 'a Python package that is not nbdev'),
 ('docker', True, False, 'there is an image to build'),
 ('deploy', False, False, ''),
 ('pages', False, False, '')]


The rest of the class acts on the catalogue and on the project’s settings. preview returns the YAML an entry would write, and add writes it into .github/workflows, refusing to replace a file that exists. generate and write_generated do the same for the one workflow gheasy builds from .gheasy/config.json. build turns a spec from the workflow builder (see wfbuild) into YAML, write_spec writes that YAML and keeps the spec beside it, and spec reads the spec back and says whether the file still matches it. docker previews the Dockerfile dockeasy detects and write_dockerfile writes it. schema returns gheasy’s env_schema, and push_env sends values for the declared keys to GitHub through the gh CLI, skipping keys the schema does not declare or that have no value.

title: wfbuild
text:
Writing GitHub Actions YAML by hand is easy to get wrong. This module builds a workflow from a spec, a small dictionary of choices that a form in a user interface can fill in: which events start the workflow, and which preset jobs it runs. compose turns the spec into YAML with gheasy’s workflow builder, and save_spec keeps the spec so the workflow can be edited later through the same form.
A spec looks like this:
{'name': 'ci', 'on': {'push': 'main', 'pull_request': 'main'},
 'jobs': [{'preset': 'uv_lint'},
          {'preset': 'uv_test', 'needs': 'lint', 'options': {'test_cmd': 'pytest -q'}}]}


source

spec_dir
def spec_dir():
The directory, relative to the repository root, where workflow specs are kept.




source

use_spec_dir
def use_spec_dir(
    dir
):
Set the directory, relative to the repository root, where workflow specs are kept.


Specs are kept as JSON files in one directory of the repository: workflows/, unless a host application picks another with use_spec_dir. spec_dir returns the directory in use. The YAML itself goes in .github/workflows/ as usual.
TRIGGERS lists the events the on part of a spec can name. Each has a label, the kind of value a form should ask for (branch names, a yes-or-no flag, or a cron expression) and a default. PRESETS lists the job types a spec can use. Each preset has an id, the job name it creates, a description and the options it accepts. preset_rows returns both lists for a user interface to render:


source

preset_rows

Form fields arrive as text or as lists. _listy splits a comma-separated value into a clean list, _lines splits a multi-line value into its non-blank lines, and _branches reads a branch field, treating True or an empty value as main:

_listy('main, dev ,'), _lines('echo one\n\n  echo two'), _branches(True)

(['main', 'dev'], ['echo one', '  echo two'], ['main'])


_triggers applies the on part of a spec to a gheasy workflow. Branch fields become branches filters, a tags value becomes a tag filter on the push trigger (v* when it is just True), and a schedule becomes a cron entry. A spec that turns on no trigger at all gets workflow_dispatch, so the workflow can at least be started by hand. The examples use on_of, a helper defined at the top of this notebook, which applies the triggers to an empty workflow and returns the rendered on block:

on_of({'push': 'main, dev', 'tags': 'v*'})

{'push': {'branches': ['main', 'dev'], 'tags': ['v*']}}


With a single trigger and no filters, gheasy writes on as a bare string instead of a mapping. That is the plain-string shape that Workflows._triggers reads back.

on_of({'push': False, 'workflow_dispatch': False})

'workflow_dispatch'

def deploy_job(
    wfb, job_id, opts, schema, app
):
Add the lego deploy job: the schema as the job’s environment, the SSH key, then the deploy command.


deploy_job adds the deploy job of the lego pattern. Every key in the schema becomes an environment variable of the job: a key whose schema value is None reads from GitHub secrets, and any other key reads from vars. DEPLOY_KEY is always added as a secret. The job checks out the code (with Git LFS files unless lfs is off), installs uv and the dependencies, writes the SSH key when there is one, and runs the deploy command:

wfb = Workflow('deploy')
deploy_job(wfb, 'deploy', {'cmd': 'python deploy.py deploy'}, {'API_KEY': None, 'REGION': 'eu'}, 'lego')
built(wfb)['jobs']['deploy']['env']

wfb = Workflow('release')
if hasattr(wfb, 'fastship_release_job'):

    test_eq(list(built(wfb)['jobs']), ['release'])
else: test_fail(lambda: fastship_job(wfb), contains='pip install -U gheasy')

def nbdev_job(
    wfb, job_id:str='test', needs:NoneType=None
):
Add nbdev’s CI job: install, run nbdev-test, then fail if nbdev-clean changes a notebook.


nbdev_job adds nbdev’s CI job. After checkout and installing with uv, it runs nbdev-test, which executes the notebooks as tests. A step named “Notebooks are clean” then runs nbdev-clean and git diff --exit-code, which fails when cleaning changed a committed notebook. nbdev 3 has no check-only flag for nbdev-clean.

wfb = Workflow('ci'); nbdev_job(wfb)
[s.get('run') or s['uses'] for s in built(wfb)['jobs']['test']['steps']]

['actions/checkout@v4',
 'astral-sh/setup-uv@v5',
 'uv sync --frozen',
 'uv run nbdev-test',
 'uv run nbdev-clean\ngit diff --exit-code']


The run preset is the catch-all. Give it commands, one per line, and each becomes a step named Step 1, Step 2 and so on. Blank lines are dropped. With no commands it runs echo hello, because GitHub rejects a job with no steps. With install off, the job keeps checkout and uv setup but skips installing the dependencies:

wfb = Workflow('ci')
_run_job(wfb, 'smoke', {'cmds': 'echo one\n\necho two', 'install': False})
[(s['name'], s.get('run') or s['uses']) for s in built(wfb)['jobs']['smoke']['steps']]

[('Checkout', 'actions/checkout@v4'),
 ('Setup uv', 'astral-sh/setup-uv@v5'),
 ('Step 1', 'echo one'),
 ('Step 2', 'echo two')]


gheasy’s preset jobs choose their own ids. _adopt renames the job just added to the id the spec asked for and attaches its needs, so that other jobs in the spec can refer to it.

compose
def compose(
    spec, schema:NoneType=None, app:str=''
):
Turn a workflow-builder spec into YAML with gheasy, giving each job a unique id.


compose turns a whole spec into YAML. It applies the triggers, then adds one job for each row of jobs from that row’s preset, passing on its options and needs. Rows that name an unknown preset are skipped. When two rows would get the same job id, the second gets a number, so two uv_test rows give test and test2. compose reads and writes no files; Workflows.build is the method that calls it for a repository:

spec = {'name': 'ci', 'on': {'push': 'main', 'pull_request': 'main'},
    'jobs': [{'preset': 'uv_lint'},
        {'preset': 'uv_test', 'needs': 'lint',
            'options': {'test_cmd': 'pytest -q', 'python_versions': '3.11, 3.12'}}]}
print(compose(spec))

title: project
text:
Before pullup can release a project it has to know what kind of project it is, because each kind is released with different commands. This module reads the marker files in a folder (settings.ini, pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml, setup_app.py) and returns the steps that release it. Nothing here runs a command or touches the network.


source

Step
def Step(
    id:str, label:str, cmd:str, doc:str='', needs:list=<factory>, argv:list=<factory>, meta:dict=<factory>
)->None:
One command in a release or deploy, with the keys it needs and the text that describes it.


A step is one command in a release, such as uploading to PyPI. Step holds what a user interface shows about it (label and doc), what to run (cmd), and the environment keys the command needs (needs). Usually cmd is the command itself and the pipeline splits it into arguments. When a command would not split correctly, such as a python -c snippet full of quotes and newlines, put the exact arguments in argv and keep cmd as the text to display. meta carries anything else a caller wants to keep with the step.
dict returns the step as a plain dictionary, with copies of its lists so that changing the result leaves the step alone. A pipeline saves its plan from these dictionaries and reads it back, argv included:

s = Step('pypi', 'PyPI release', 'python -m twine upload dist/*',
         'Upload the built distributions to PyPI.', ['TWINE_USERNAME', 'TWINE_PASSWORD'])
s.dict()

{'id': 'pypi',
 'label': 'PyPI release',
 'cmd': 'python -m twine upload dist/*',
 'doc': 'Upload the built distributions to PyPI.',
 'needs': ['TWINE_USERNAME', 'TWINE_PASSWORD'],
 'argv': [],
 'meta': {}}

nbdev_project
def nbdev_project(
    root
):
Whether root is an nbdev project, by its nbdev 2 settings.ini or its pyproject.toml.


Each detector answers one yes-or-no question about a folder:

nbdev_project: an nbdev library, declared by an nbdev 2 settings.ini, a [tool.nbdev] table in pyproject.toml, or an nbdev entry point there.
rust_project: a Rust crate, which means there is a Cargo.toml.
maturin_project: a Rust crate that maturin also builds into a Python wheel, so its release goes to PyPI.
fastship_project: a Python package with a pyproject.toml that is not an nbdev library. fastship is the release tool for such packages.
app_project: a project that also builds a desktop app, recognised by setup_app.py together with tools/build_release.py.

A pyproject.toml that is missing or is not valid TOML counts as empty instead of raising, so a half-written file never stops detection.

lib   = mkproj('a_notebook_lib', {'settings.ini': '[DEFAULT]\nlib_name = demo\nnbs_path = nbs\n'})
crate = mkproj('a_crate', {'Cargo.toml': '[package]\nname = "demo"\n'})
pkg   = mkproj('a_package', {'pyproject.toml': '[project]\nname = "demo"\n'})
[(p.name, nbdev_project(p), rust_project(p), fastship_project(p)) for p in (lib, crate, pkg)]

[('a_notebook_lib', True, False, False),
 ('a_crate', False, True, False),
 ('a_package', False, False, True)]


Each kind of project has its own list of steps. NBDEV_STEPS, FASTSHIP_STEPS, PLAIN_STEPS, MATURIN_STEPS and CRATE_STEPS are those lists, and FLOWS maps a flow name to its list. Pass your own mapping to default_steps or Project to change what a flow runs.
APP_STEPS is not a flow of its own. Its two steps build the desktop app and attach it to the GitHub release, and they are added to whichever flow the project uses. A maturin release uploads nothing from your machine: it pushes a tag, and CI builds and publishes a wheel for every platform.
These are the step ids of each flow, then the keys the fastship steps need:

{name: [s.id for s in steps] for name, steps in FLOWS.items()}

{'nbdev': ['prepare', 'bump', 'gh', 'pypi'],
 'fastship': ['test', 'changelog', 'gh', 'pypi', 'bump'],
 'plain': ['test', 'build', 'gh', 'pypi'],
 'maturin': ['test', 'wheel', 'ci', 'changelog', 'release'],
 'crate': ['test', 'clippy', 'package', 'publish']}



{s.id: s.needs for s in FASTSHIP_STEPS if s.needs}

{'changelog': ['GITHUB_TOKEN'],
 'gh': ['GITHUB_TOKEN'],
 'pypi': ['TWINE_USERNAME', 'TWINE_PASSWORD']}

release_flow
def release_flow(
    root
):
The name of the release flow that fits the project in root.


release_flow names the flow for a folder. It checks for nbdev first, then for maturin before a plain Rust crate (every maturin project is also a crate), then for fastship. Anything else, including a folder that does not exist, is plain.
default_steps returns that flow’s steps. For a project that builds a desktop app it inserts the app steps straight after the last gh or pypi step, so any step after those still runs last; a flow with neither gets them at the end.

[(p.name, release_flow(p)) for p in (lib, crate, pkg, root/'no_such_folder')]

[('a_notebook_lib', 'nbdev'),
 ('a_crate', 'crate'),
 ('a_package', 'fastship'),
 ('no_such_folder', 'plain')]



app = mkproj('a_desktop_app', {'pyproject.toml': '[project]\nname = "demo"\n',
                               'setup_app.py': '', 'tools/build_release.py': ''})
[s.id for s in default_steps(app)]

['test', 'changelog', 'gh', 'pypi', 'app', 'assets', 'bump']


The app steps land after pypi and before bump, because fastship raises the version for the next cycle only once the release is out.

Project
def Project(
    root, flows:NoneType=None
):
The kind of project one folder holds and the steps that release it.


Project wraps all of this for one folder. It resolves the path once, when you create it, but works out kind and packages_an_app again each time you ask, so it notices files added since. steps returns the release steps and dict returns everything as JSON-ready data for a user interface.

p = Project(pkg)
d = p.dict()
p, d['kind'], d['app'], [s['id'] for s in d['steps']]

(Project(a_package, fastship),
 'fastship',
 False,
 ['test', 'changelog', 'gh', 'pypi', 'bump'])
